articles.title: How medical neglect killed Alfredo Díaz in a Venezuelan cell
articles.author: Luis Carlos Diaz
paras: The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs
Originally published on Global Voices
Illustration made with AI by Runrunes. Used with permission.
Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission. Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles.

To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed. Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”

Despite the Venezuelan state’s complete refusal to cooperate, the FFM’s technical findings expose a crucial reality. Following the United States’ military intervention on January 3 and the capture of Nicolás Maduro, interim president Delcy Rodríguez announced cabinet reshuffles, released hundreds of prisoners, and oversaw a decline in long-term detentions.

However, the United Nations (UN) found that at least 18 high-ranking officials previously implicated in human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain in key positions of power or military command, including Diosdado Cabello, Gustavo González López, Alexander Granko Arteaga, and Vladimir Padrino López. The core architecture of state repression remains fully intact, providing the structural context for the individual cases documented in this series.

Before delving into the case of Alfredo Díaz, I want to address a question that often lingers when we discuss the UN reports: What is all this work actually for? What happens to a report like this once it is published?

The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission was not created on a whim, nor was it meant to issue a general diagnosis and stop there. It was established by the Human Rights Council under Resolution 42/25 in 2019, with a specific mandate: to document the most serious crimes committed in the country to combat impunity, ensure accountability for those responsible, and secure justice for victims. This carries practical consequences, even if they are not immediate.

The FFM is an investigative body, one of only seven active mechanisms of its kind worldwide. That alone underscores how extraordinary our situation is, and how resilient civil society has been in organizing to secure its renewal on four separate occasions. In October, countries in the Human Rights Council voted to extend its mandate for two additional years.

Whenever the FFM concludes there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that an individual participated in a human rights violation, that finding is preserved in secure databases with case files, testimonies, and evidence. This material is not lost, even if no Venezuelan court is willing to use it.

This documentation has already had real effects outside Venezuela. The report notes, for instance, that a federal court in Argentina issued an extradition request in June 2026 against a Spain-based former Venezuelan military officer linked to the 2014 repression. The court relied on the principle of universal jurisdiction — the legal framework allowing a country to prosecute grave international crimes committed elsewhere, when justice is denied in the country of origin. That officer was named in the 2025 special report on the Bolivarian National Guard.

Furthermore, although Venezuela formally denounced the Rome Statute in July 2026 in an attempt to block cooperation with the International Criminal Court, the FFM’s report clarifies a crucial point: a withdrawal from the ICC does not erase or halt ongoing investigations by the tribunal in The Hague for events that occurred while the statute was still in force for the country. In other words, these reports have allowed us to build, fact by fact, the evidentiary record that may one day support a criminal indictment inside or outside Venezuela. This is why more victims and witnesses should be encouraged to share their stories with the FFM.

With that purpose in mind, reading the case of Alfredo Díaz is well worth the effort. Díaz was a former governor of Nueva Esparta and a regional leader of the Acción Democrática party. SEBIN officers arrested him on November 24, 2024, in Ospino, Portuguesa state, leaving his family completely unaware of his whereabouts for four days. This marked the start of multiple due process violations, including incommunicado detention and enforced disappearance. Charged with “incitement to hatred” and “terrorism,” he spent the remainder of his detention unable to appoint defense counsel of his choice or access his own case file.

What makes this case particularly grave, according to the FFM, is not only the arbitrary detention (a serious crime in itself), but what happened to his health. Before his arrest, Díaz had a history of serious medical conditions, including seizures, an anxiety disorder with paranoid traits, and depression. A medical report from that year included pending orders for pharmacological treatment, a CT scan, and a neurological evaluation. The political persecution he suffered rendered him unable to maintain his medical care.

Witnesses who shared a cell with him reported that he suffered at least two severe medical episodes while incarcerated. One occurred in October 2025 and was characterized by intense pain, muscle stiffness, and disorientation, which medical personnel at El Helicoide diagnosed as “indigestion” and a “stomach issue.” No specialist ever evaluated Díaz, the FFM documented, despite repeated pleas from his family and fellow inmates. Such negligence extends the punishment beyond detainees to their loved ones, who remain impotent to help, forced to advocate from a distance.

On December 6, 2025, at around 5:00 a.m. local time, Díaz experienced the same symptoms. His cellmates’ desperate alarms were met with a delayed response. Díaz was eventually transferred to the facility’s medical area, where staff performed resuscitation maneuvers, but he died shortly after at the University Hospital of Caracas. The official cause of death was listed as an acute myocardial infarction.

The FFM is not asserting that Díaz was beaten to death or that a direct order was issued to let him die. Instead, it points to something that is, in many ways, more difficult for state officials to evade: the sustained lack of specialized medical care, despite clear warning signs — repeated for more than a year — was a contributing factor in his death. This constitutes an arbitrary deprivation of life attributable to the state, which inherits a strict obligation to protect the health and life of anyone it takes into custody.

This brings us to the key connection between this case and the core finding mentioned at the start of this series. Díaz was not an isolated case. The FFM also documented the death in custody of Edison José Torres Fernández, a police officer with 24 years of service who was detained for criticizing the government, and whose body bore bruises that went unacknowledged in the official death certificate.

These are distinct stories unfolding within the same detention system and reflecting the same underlying pattern: people incarcerated with known medical conditions left in a coffin, with no one held accountable to date.

articles.title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional
articles.author: Janine Mendes-Franco
paras: ‘The law finally caught up with basic human dignity’
Originally published on Global Voices

Trinbagonian LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones at the Hall of Justice in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after the landmark 2018 judgement that deemed Trinidad and Tobago’s ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional. Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.

It has been a long road to get to this point. Almost as soon as the 2018 judgement went in Jones’ favour, the Trinidad and Tobago government announced its intention to appeal, with then Attorney General Faris Al-Rawi stating, “The rights of equality in the Constitution are clearly expressed. A first-instance decision is not the only decision to rely upon to settle the law. [An appeal] is only prudent so we can conclusively put the matter to rest.”

Almost seven years later, on March 25, 2025, a local appeal court overturned the 2018 judgement. Jones was disappointed but not deterred, vowing to take the case all the way to the Privy Council. He remained true to his word and on November 10, 2026 — quite ironically, given that it was a colonial-era law — British lawlords finally ruled on the matter.

There were a few key issues to be considered, including how to address the controversial “savings law” clause in the legislation — laws enacted prior to colonised countries becoming independent and developing their own constitutions, that were “saved” to remain in force even afterwards. Jones maintained that the clause had “no place in a 21st century democracy” and that Trinidad and Tobago’s government and parliament were “derelict” in not removing it, especially after the twin-island nation became a republic in 1976.

The Council’s conclusion in the case, which deemed that “Sections 13 and 16 of the SOA 1986 have been shown by Mr Jones ‘not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual,’” caused it to agree with the 2018 ruling and deny the attorney-general’s cross-appeal.

With other regional territories also using the Privy Council as their highest court of appeal, the result could augur well for similar actions across the wider Caribbean. As Jones told reporters on the steps of Trinidad’s Hall of Justice following his 2018 triumph, “The human rights issue is not just local […] Over 75 million Commonwealth citizens are criminalised using similar laws — 37 Commonwealth nations — criminalised similarly to Trinidad.”

Still, Jones — who launched his legal challenge in 2015 — says that the fight continues: “Whilst I welcome this judgement, it does not, however, address the main issues of human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial-era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond.” It is a stance echoed by many LGBTQ+ organisations, as issues of discrimination, language, and societal and religious acceptance also persist. Jones is well aware that changing these attitudes requires broader reform and re-education.
The law lords’ unanimous, provisional view, however, was that the original High Court remedy should stand. However, there may well be written submissions still to come.

Reactions from both within and beyond the LGBTQ+ community soon followed. Facebook user Ian Ragoonanan described the Privy Council ruling as “the law finally [catching] up with basic human dignity,” while academic Richard Drayton felt that the most important paragraph in the Privy Council judgement read: “[T]he rights in Sections 4 and 5 of the Constitution develop over time, since the Constitution is a living instrument capable of reflecting contemporaneous understandings of constitutional values […] The longer the passage of time, the more likely it is that those values will have developed in modern society and the more likely it is that the Constitution has to be interpreted accordingly.”

Pride TT, meanwhile, celebrated the victory: “We salute Jason Jones for his courage, resilience and unwavering determination, and recognise the advocates, allies and organisations who have stood alongside this fight for justice.” More than a mere legal milestone, it said, the judgement was “a reminder that everyone deserves to live with dignity, privacy and freedom from discrimination.”

articles.title: Ecuadorian youth unite against neoliberal models and state violence
articles.author: Gina Yauri
paras: Students are demanding a just future for all
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of X video of the October 10, 2026 protest in Quito, Ecuador. Video by X user Elena Rodríguez. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.

Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador. Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center. The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:

Lo que pasa en Quito es impresionante: Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse. Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv — Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 10, 2026

What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse. Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents. Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
Structural failures driving youth mobilization

According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old. Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month. The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million. The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.
Slogans as the language of youth resistance

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.

Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest. Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

Estoy harta de tener que narrar, una y otra vez, las agresiones policiales contra la prensa. Hoy, mientras intentaba documentar la violencia con la que los agentes golpeaban a jóvenes manifestantes, recibí por la espalda un toletazo en la cabeza. Me di la vuelta, mostré mi micrófono de teleSUR para identificarme como periodista y la respuesta fue otro toletazo que terminó partiéndolo. Los periodistas no queremos ser noticia. Yo no quiero ser protagonista de nada. Estoy en las calles para contar lo que ocurre, para documentar aquello que el poder muchas veces preferiría que nadie viera. Y si creen que a punta de golpes van a conseguir que deje de registrar la brutalidad policial, que aparte mi micrófono o que me repliegue varias cuadras para ejercer el periodismo desde donde no incomode, se equivocan. No somos los periodistas quienes debemos alejarnos de los hechos. Son los policías quienes deben dejar de agredir. El derecho a informar no se negocia a punta de tolete. — Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 11, 2026

I am fed up with having to recount, time and again, police assaults against the press. Today, while attempting to document the violence with which officers were beating young protesters, I was struck on the back of the head with a baton. I turned around and held up my teleSUR microphone to identify myself as a journalist; the response was another blow from a baton, which ended up shattering it. We journalists do not want to be the news. I have no desire to be the protagonist of anything. I am out on the streets to report on what is happening — to document things that those in power would often prefer no one to see. And if they think that by using force — by raining down blows — they can make me stop recording police brutality, force me to put away my microphone, or push me back several blocks so that I might practice journalism from a place where I won’t cause any ‘inconvenience,’ they are sorely mistaken. It is not the journalists who should step away from the events; it is the police who must stop the assaults. The right to report cannot be negotiated at the end of a baton.
Hatari Ulcuango, President of the Federation of Students of the Catholic University of Ecuador, warned in one of his speeches that these mobilizations were “just the beginning.”

On October 10, as young people occupied the streets with their marches and sit-ins, they also used art to make their voices heard, singing songs, playing musical instruments, wearing masks, and dressing up in costumes. In doing so, they demonstrated that together, they can be very strong and that violence is not needed to speak one’s mind.

The government responded by sending the authorities to quell the protests and repress the demonstrators. Denunciations of the outcomes of state violence — dozens of students suffocated, injured, and detained — quickly spread across social media. These young people promised, however, that as long as they go unheard and continue to be treated with the blunt coercion of the state, they will return to the streets and not falter.

The leading role of youth in the streets of Ecuador, pitted against the state’s capacity for violent repression, evidence not only the crisis of the social state and the consolidation of an exclusionary state, but also the historical role of young people as agents of political change.

The glass generation — the one society has tried to shield — is experiencing the contradictions of an economic and political system that excludes them, making their future increasingly uncertain, and they are doing something about it.

articles.title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?
articles.author: Sandra Tuombouh
paras: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empowering community members
Originally published on Global Voices
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm. Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon. Used with permission.

Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year. Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September. Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.

Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families. Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment. More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.

Children are among those affected. Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition. Beyond its nutritional consequences, food insecurity can also affect children’s ability to learn and participate in school activities.

According to the Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO), hunger can impair concentration and memory and affect classroom attendance. In February 2026, the organisation reported that only 2.8 percent of primary school pupils in Cameroon received a free hot meal at school, highlighting the limited reach of school lunch programmes.
Conflict, climate-related disasters, agricultural losses and rising staple food prices are among the main drivers of this crisis.
To combat persistent food insecurity, educators and nonprofit organisations are partnering to teach children how to grow their own food.

In Bamenda, North West region of Cameroon, the Youth Association for Climate Action (YACA) runs the ADAPT Programme, which engages 70 pupils from two nursery and primary schools. Created after a survey revealed that few schools had gardens or provided environmental education, the ADAPT Club has established gardens with five sections: nurseries, vegetables, fruit trees, composting and tubers.

Muluh Kelly Vughose, Programme coordinator for ADAPT, says pupils are involved in more than just planting. “Our volunteers, together with the teachers and pupils, designed each garden. Children are also involved in learning basic agricultural skills like plantain propagation and grafting of fruit trees.” The club holds two sessions each week, lasting about two hours.

In the same region, in Nkambe and neighbouring villages, pupils from six primary and two secondary schools are learning agricultural skills through the Smart School Gardens Project, launched by Youth Development Organisation – Yodo Cameroon. Schools have received wheelbarrows, watering cans and compost manure to support the project.

“During the two years of implementation, I have watched these pupils and students care for plants from seed germination until harvest,” says Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s Programme Coordinator. The gardens produce cabbage, huckleberry, carrots and Irish potatoes.

Meanwhile, SUHUCAM’s regenerative school garden programme in the Centre region combines fruit trees, including guava, soursop, orange and papaya, with plantains and produce such as huckleberry, cabbage and waterleaf. Through these activities, pupils are learning techniques such as composting, plant propagation and grafting.

Children are embracing the school gardens with enthusiasm, discovering the importance of food production and sustainability through practical experience. Queeninver Ngwangung, SUHUCAM’s Youth and Advocacy Lead, explains:

“Rather than simply teaching students about sustainable agriculture, food security or climate action, we give them opportunities to practice these concepts,” she said. “Through growing food, managing organic waste and caring for their gardens, we have observed that students have learnt that environmental solutions can begin with everyday actions within their own schools.”

For Amang Mael, a Form Three student, seeing vegetables grow on an abandoned plot behind his school has been particularly exciting. “Since we planted the vegetables, I have been so eager to harvest. We add organic manure to all our crops so they can be healthy.”

Another student, Kouba Princesse, believes the garden can contribute to the fight against hunger. “Now that I know how to grow my own vegetables, I will not have to depend on buying from the market all the time,” she says. Some kids have taken the practice home, where they maintain small gardens and use plastic bottles for drip irrigation during the dry season. Other students also say the experience has sparked an interest in pursuing careers in agriculture.
Supporting community nutrition

In 2025, the ADAPT Club produced approximately 45 kilogrammes of dry compost from biodegradable waste. At the end of each planting cycle, YACA organises a Mini School Garden Market Day, where parents and community members can buy the harvest. “Income gained is reinvested in the next planting cycle,” says Muluh Kelly.

At SUHUCAM, the harvests serve nutritional and educational purposes. Students eat fruits from the gardens, while vegetables are sold to purchase seeds and fund their continued management. Some students take extra produce home to establish household gardens.
After two years with two regenerative school garden cycles, SUHUCAM’s Climate Change and Innovation Club has benefitted thousands of households and planted over 400 trees.

In Nkambe, pupils involved in Yodo Cameroon’s project also sell their harvests to community members at affordable prices. The proceeds have helped schools purchase basic educational materials, including chalk and exercise books. Ekoaba Cevie, Yodo Cameroon’s project manager says:

The gardens have become practical outdoor classrooms. Not only are the children learning new agricultural skills, but they are also gaining an appreciation for nature, responsible environmental practices and sustainable resource management.

The nutritional potential of school-based production is also evident in other initiatives. In 2025, an integrated school production programme supported by FAO in Cameroon’s East and South regions established 18 school gardens. The programme produced 236,859 kilogrammes of vegetables, alongside eggs and fish, helping provide weekly healthy meals to 10,833 students. Children, teachers and community members also received training in sustainable agriculture, hygiene and nutrition.

Nkimih Clinton, a researcher at the Institute of Agricultural Research for Development (IRAD), says regenerative practices, such as those deployed in the community gardens, can improve soil health and support sustainable agriculture. Composting, mulching, crop rotation and organic manure, he explains, “can contribute to maintaining the health of pieces of land” for crop production. However, he cautions against expecting small-scale school gardens to eliminate hunger entirely.

Although they may not provide all the food pupils need, they can improve dietary quality by supplying vegetables, legumes and fruits rich in essential vitamins and minerals. “School gardens can be used as a source of production of micro-nutrients to complement basic staples (cassava, maize, rice) provided by parents,” Clinton says.

Despite their benefits, maintaining school gardens remains difficult. Programme coordinators say unpredictable rainfall makes it harder to plan planting activities and sustain crop production. Changing weather conditions can also contribute to pest outbreaks and seed shortages.

Maintaining the gardens during school holidays is another challenge, as pupils are less available to care for the crops. These difficulties can interrupt children’s opportunities to follow the entire production cycle, from planting to harvesting. Expanding the initiatives will therefore require coordinated support from government officials, agricultural research institutions and development partners.
Schools need funding, reliable water supply, farming tools, quality seeds and technical assistance to maintain productive gardens throughout the year.
Government and policy support

Cameroon has previously taken steps to promote environmental education in schools. In 2018, the Ministry of Secondary Education and the Israeli Ambassador to Cameroon launched a Green School campaign that planted 300 trees in 30 schools.

In May 2023, the country launched the second phase of the Classes Vertes project, a three-year initiative developed by FAO in partnership with the Special Council Support Fund for Mutual Assistance (FEICOM) and several government ministries. Targeting 80 schools across the Far North, North, Adamawa, East and South regions, the programme sought to promote vegetable production, fish farming and poultry farming to improve children’s access to nutritious food. It also included tree planting and initiatives to build school canteens, water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities, with an allocated budget of approximately FCFA 722 million (USD 1.2 million).

The government’s commitment to improving children’s access to nutritious food is also reflected in its National School Feeding Strategy for 2025–2030, which aims to expand school meals and strengthen links between schools and local food producers.

Officials hope the program will reach one million learners by 2030. In July 2026, the government, through the Ministry of Basic Education, signed a EUR 3.6 million (USD 4 million) agreement with the World Food Programme (WFP) to expand home-grown school feeding in the Adamawa, East and Far North regions. The 2026–2029 programme is expected to provide nutritious meals to nearly 11,000 children in ten public primary schools while creating market opportunities for 600 smallholder farmers.

Meanwhile, experts believe school gardens can be replicated across Cameroon but stress that their implementation must reflect the country’s different agro-ecological zones. Rather than adopting a uniform approach, schools need solutions suited to their agro-ecological zones.

While school gardens may not independently resolve Cameroon’s food insecurity challenges, they offer opportunities to strengthen children’s nutritional knowledge, promote sustainable agriculture and encourage household food production. Their long-term impact, however, will depend on sustained investment, technical support and policies that enable more schools to establish and maintain these initiatives.

articles.title: From ancient Asia to the AI age: Has China’s ‘beauty stratagem’ found a new victim in Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
articles.author: Linggong Kong, Ph.D. Candidate in Political Science, Auburn University
paras: Extramarital activities have led to the resignation of one of America’s most influential tech bosses, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The saga has also raised the specter of an age-old spying tactic: the “honey trap.”

Huang stepped down following media reports of an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence agencies. She previously worked for Megaspeed, a cloud computing company under U.S. scrutiny for allegedly helping China obtain restricted AI chips.
Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair. And amid reports of a second with a company executive who reports to him, he tendered his resignation to the Nvidia board on Nov. 12, 2026.

The sensitivity of Huang’s work – AI is increasingly seen as central to national security – has turned a company matter into an international issue. China’s Foreign Ministry has denied the espionage allegations and accused the U.S. of “fabricating so-called spy narratives and ⁠⁠⁠⁠using them as a pretext for imposing ⁠⁠⁠⁠a technological blockade.” Nvidia says it has no reason to believe company secrets have been leaked.
Yet part of what makes the accusations so believable is history is dotted with examples of men being distracted, compromised or spied on by attractive men and women deployed for that purpose.
Indeed, in China it recalls an ancient political tactic known as “meiren ji” or the “beauty stratagem.”

As a scholar specializing in U.S.-China relations, I believe that regardless of the particulars of the Huang case, the political logic behind the beauty stratagem – using personal relationships to obtain information, influence decisions and weaken opponents – remains relevant today. As such, it would be no surprise if the tactic was being used amid the growing U.S.-China competition over AI and advanced semiconductors.
The beauty stratagem of Ancient China

“Meiren ji” is one of “Thirty-Six Stratagems,” a Chinese military text of uncertain origin but generally believed to have derived from oral and written histories from the Warring States period — 475–221 BCE. Its 31st stratagem states that personal relationships can be used to influence political opponents and recommends exploiting an adversary’s personal desires and emotional vulnerabilities to weaken their judgment and undermine their leadership.
The “Thirty-Six Stratagems” is both a playbook for warfare and a reflection on past experience.
Indeed, one of China’s most famous beauty stratagem stories dates back more than 2,000 years to the Spring and Autumn period of Chinese history.

In the fifth century BCE, King Goujian of Yue, in modern-day southern China, was defeated by King Fuchai of Wu, its northern neighbor, and forced to submit. But Goujian secretly rebuilt his strength and prepared for revenge.
According to the ancient historical text “Wu Yue Chun Qiu,” Yue sent two beautiful women – Xi Shi and Zheng Dan – to Fuchai, hoping he would become distracted by pleasure and neglect state affairs.
The plan reportedly worked. Fuchai, seemingly enchanted by the beautiful women, gradually ignored Yue’s threat. Meanwhile, Goujian prepared for war and in 473 BCE Yue conquered Wu.
Xi Shi’s actual role in Wu’s downfall remains unclear. Wu’s defeat involved poor political decisions and Yue’s military recovery.
Still, the story illustrated an important idea in Chinese political strategy: exploiting an opponent’s personal weaknesses can sometimes be more effective than confronting him directly.
A similar tactic appears in the 14th-century novel “Romance of the Three Kingdoms,” considered one of the classics of Chinese literature.

It tells the story of Dong Zhuo, a powerful warlord who controlled the imperial court during the late Eastern Han Dynasty. To remove him, Wang Yun, a senior court official loyal to the Han Dynasty promised a beautiful young woman, named Diaochan, in marriage to Dong Zhuo’s military commander. He then offered the same woman to Dong Zhuo.

The scheme fueled jealousy and distrust between the two men, eventually enabling Wang Yun to persuade Dong Zhuo’s underling to kill him. Wang Yun then briefly took charge of the imperial court on behalf of the Han emperor.
The ‘honey trap’ of modern spyware

In modern intelligence operations, using romantic or sexual relationships to approach targets, obtain sensitive information or exert influence is commonly called a “honey trap.” It is, moreover, certainly not unique to China. Western and Soviet intelligence agencies used intimate relationships for espionage frequently during the Cold War.

Modern China also has documented cases. One example involves French diplomat Bernard Boursicot and the Chinese opera performer Shi Pei Pu. The pair met in Beijing in 1964 and maintained a long-term intimate relationship. Throughout, Boursicot was providing French diplomatic documents to China. The spying was eventually exposed and both involved were prosecuted for espionage in France in the 1980s.

A more recent example involves former U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Swalwell acknowledged in 2015 that he had been physically intimate with Fang on several occasions. At the time, Fang helped raise funds for Swalwell’s campaign and helped place an intern in his congressional office.
Why Jensen Huang is strategically important

Jensen Huang’s position would make him a prime target for such a “honey trap” operation. His company has become central to the technological competition between the U.S and China. As AI becomes increasingly important to economic development, military capabilities and national security, moreover, Washington has repeatedly tightened restrictions on advanced AI chip exports to China, hoping to slow its access to computing power.
Beijing is investing heavily in domestic semiconductor development. Yet Chinese companies still need advanced chips to train AI models and build data centers.
From Beijing’s perspective, advanced AI chips matter not only for Chinese technology companies but for future military and technological competition.
This puts Nvidia in a particularly important position and helps explain the national security concerns surrounding Huang.

However, strategic motives do not prove an intelligence operation occurred. Jensen Huang’s importance does not, in itself, establish that he was targeted by a honey trap or that Alice Huang acted for Chinese intelligence. Those are allegations that still require full investigation.
Espionage in the age of AI

Yet it is surely true that in modern politics – just as in ancient China’s rivalries – rivals seek information about opponents, try to influence important decisions and exploit weaknesses to gain strategic advantages.
What has changed is who controls important strategic resources.

In ancient China, influencing a ruler through personal relationships could affect a country’s political and military decisions. Today, approaching a major technology executive could offer access to sensitive technologies.
More than 2,000 years ago, a powerful state could lose its advantage through a ruler’s personal weaknesses. Today, political and technological power are distributed differently.
But as long as important decisions depend on individuals, personal relationships may remain a weakness that rivals can exploit.

articles.title: ‘Plenty of reasons for hope’: what 30 years of climate talks have achieved
articles.author: Grace Jennings-Edquist, Executive Producer, Podcasts, The Conversation
paras: Thousands of delegates, scientists and world leaders are gathered in Turkey for the latest United Nations climate summit, COP31. Their task is familiar: agree on how to cut greenhouse gas emissions and help countries cope with a warming planet.

But after more than three decades of negotiations, global emissions remain stubbornly high and the world is on course to overshoot the critical threshold of 1.5°C of warming. So have these annual summits actually achieved anything?
Dr Wesley Morgan, a climate diplomacy expert at UNSW Sydney, tells The Conversation Weekly podcast the answer is yes:
The Paris Agreement is a monumental diplomatic achievement.
Agreed in 2015, the treaty brought more than 190 countries together around shared climate goals. Morgan says it has helped shift the trajectory of global warming:
We were headed towards utter catastrophe. We’re still headed towards some very dire circumstances and more ambition is needed, but it is better than it would have been without this global agreement.
This year’s summit presents a particular diplomatic challenge for Australia because its climate and energy minister, Chris Bowen, is leading the negotiations.

Morgan says Australia can “tell a very positive story about what’s happening domestically in Australia”, including by pointing to significant strides in rooftop solar, which is now installed on one in three homes.
But Australia’s role as President of Negotiations at COP31 is controversial because Australia remains one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and gas.
“It really is a tightrope,” Morgan says.

In September, the federal government approved an expansion of BHP’s Saraji coal mine in Queensland, while authorities in New South Wales gave the green light for a major Hunter Valley coal mine to keep operating until 2045.
The negotiations also face a major setback following the Trump administration’s withdrawal in January from international climate cooperation.
Yet Morgan notes that no other country has followed the United States out of the talks.
Pressure from Europe and the Pacific

European countries are expected to push for stronger commitments and stronger ambition from the COP 31 negotiations, following a summer of severe heatwaves and wildfires across the continent. “I think across Europe and in the UK, there’s a realisation that this is a clear and present danger now,” says Morgan.

He also points to the influence of Pacific island nations as evidence that smaller countries can shape global agreements. In 2015, The Republic of the Marshall Islands helped build the High Ambition Coalition, which was instrumental in securing the Paris Agreement and its 1.5°C goal.
For Pacific countries, Morgan says, that target is a matter of survival:
The rallying cry from the Pacific is 1.5 to stay alive.
One possible outcome from COP31 is a new global electrification target dubbed “35 by 35”: meeting 35% of the world’s final energy demand with electricity by 2035.
Morgan sees it as another step towards economies powered by clean energy – and despite the setbacks, he insists the transition is already underway:
There’s plenty of reasons for hope as well as reasons for despair.
Wesley Morgan is a fellow at the Climate Council of Australia.

articles.title: Justice is the infrastructure the world keeps forgetting
articles.author: Guest Contributor
paras: The world cannot build prosperous economies, peaceful societies or resilient democracies while neglecting its people’s everyday justice needs.
Originally published on Global Voices

This post by Jude Udo Ilo is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Imagine visiting a hospital with a serious illness, only to discover that every patient receives the same medication, regardless of their symptoms. We would rightly call this a failure of healthcare. Yet this is remarkably close to how justice is delivered in much of the world.

We have built justice systems around institutions rather than people, procedures rather than problems, and legal traditions rather than lived realities. We measure progress by the number of courts constructed, judges appointed and laws enacted, while paying insufficient attention to whether ordinary people can actually resolve the disputes disrupting their lives.

This institutional obsession reflects a deeper failure in how we understand development. Justice is not simply a legal service or a moral aspiration. It is essential for economic and social infrastructure. Our collective failure to treat it as such is undermining development, deepening inequality and threatening global stability. With the level of discontent across the world, distrust in institutions, poverty and inequality, and growing footprints of violent conflict, we need to refocus on what is necessary to heal our bleeding world.
The missing infrastructure of development

When governments and international financial institutions discuss infrastructure, the conversation invariably turns to roads, bridges, electricity and digital connectivity. These investments matter. But what happens when a highway project becomes trapped in unresolved land disputes; when a small business cannot recover payments from a supplier? When a woman cannot claim her inheritance, or communities cannot secure remedies for environmental destruction?

Physical infrastructure cannot deliver its promised benefits when the institutions and mechanisms for resolving grievances are inaccessible, ineffective or distrusted. Justice is the soft infrastructure that allows economies and societies to function.

For businesses, it provides the certainty necessary for investment, contract enforcement and growth. For individuals, it protects rights, livelihoods and opportunities. For communities, it creates peaceful pathways for addressing grievances before they escalate into confrontation.

Without functioning justice systems, economic development becomes fragile and social stability increasingly precarious. The World Justice Project estimates that the economic costs of legal problems, including lost income, health impacts and expenses of seeking resolution, average 1.7 percent of GDP across the countries studied.

The scale of the problem is staggering. The Justice for All report estimates that 5.2 billion people lack meaningful access to justice. HiiL's research demonstrates that everyday legal problems are widespread, while effective, satisfactory resolutions remain elusive. This is a crisis of development.
When injustice becomes insecurity
Across the world, unresolved grievances are quietly eroding the foundations of social cohesion.

In parts of Africa, disputes over land ownership, natural resources and community rights have contributed to recurring tensions. In fragile and conflict-affected societies, the absence of credible mechanisms for resolving grievances can deepen mistrust and reinforce cycles of violence.

But justice failures are hardly confined to developing countries. From housing disputes and discriminatory employment practices to unequal access to legal representation, even wealthy democracies struggle to ensure that justice works for everyone.

The consequences extend beyond those directly affected. When people repeatedly encounter institutions that cannot protect their rights or resolve their problems, confidence in public authority deteriorates. When people encounter injustice, they can easily become the enemy of the state. And where legitimate institutions fail, alternative systems of enforcement emerge. Sometimes these are constructive community mechanisms. At other times, they involve coercion, exploitation or violence. We cannot sustainably address insecurity while ignoring the injustices that help fuel it.

This should fundamentally change how governments approach peacebuilding and security. Military and policing investments may respond to immediate threats, but accessible justice can help address grievances before they become security crises.
Justice should therefore be understood as preventive infrastructure, not merely a mechanism for responding to wrongdoing after it occurs.
What the evidence tells us

Fortunately, evidence from across HiiL’s global operations demonstrates how people-centred approaches are transforming the design and delivery of justice services. Rather than relying solely on formal courtrooms or conventional approaches to conflict resolution, community-led initiatives and alternative justice pathways are meeting people where their disputes actually occur.

In Kenya, research informed the Judiciary’s Social Transformation through Access to Justice (STAJ) Blueprint. The Alternative Justice Systems (AJS) centres in Kenya are resolving family, land and other disputes locally, thereby preserving community cohesion. In Ethiopia, government-led community justice centers bridge formal laws and customary traditions to deliver rapid, reconciliation-focused resolution. In Nigeria, pilot community justice centers and domestic violence one-stop shops in Imo and Ogun States provide scalable, data-driven dispute resolution. In Tunisia, digital platforms co-developed for employment disputes directly connect workers, employers, and inspectors to resolve conflicts before they escalate.
Instead of assuming what institutions need, the question is: What justice problems do people actually experience, and what would help resolve them fairly?

Through Justice Needs and Satisfaction (JNS) surveys, we gather data on everyday legal experiences rather than institutional outputs. The data consistently reveal a significant disconnect between supply and demand. In Tunisia, we found that nearly one in three adults experiences a legal problem annually, yet only a fraction reach formal courts. Similarly, research in Nigeria highlights widespread justice needs alongside heavy reliance on community and informal mechanisms. These insights expose the core limitation of traditional justice reform: expanding court capacity alone cannot solve the problem. People facing family, land, employment, or commercial disputes rarely seek lengthy litigation. They need solutions that are fair, accessible, affordable, and timely.

Similar approaches are yielding results. In Bangladesh, a government-led initiative has strengthened village courts, enabling rural communities to resolve minor disputes locally, more quickly and affordably. These courts resolved over 82 percent of reported cases in an average of 25 days, at an average cost of just USD 2.70 to users. In Canada, the Indigenous Justice Program supports community-based initiatives that involve Indigenous communities in designing and delivering culturally appropriate justice services, reflecting their needs and traditions. In Colombia, Houses of Justice bring together formal and informal justice services, providing communities with access to legal information, mediation and dispute resolution through integrated service centres. These examples illustrate how justice services can be brought closer to people and organised around different pathways to better respond to their needs.

This does not make courts obsolete; rather, it underscores that formal courts are only one component of a healthy justice ecosystem. To truly serve society, functional justice infrastructure must integrate formal institutions with trusted community mechanisms, mediation, legal support, and innovative services.
From justice reform to justice investment
If justice is infrastructure, we must fundamentally rethink how we finance, govern and deliver it.

First, governments must stop treating justice as the Ministry of Justice's exclusive responsibility. Economic planners, finance ministries, development institutions, businesses and peacebuilding organisations all have a stake in effective dispute resolution.

Second, justice investments must be guided by evidence about people's needs and outcomes. HiiL's Delivering Justice, Rigorously framework emphasises data, evidence-based practices, scalable services, enabling environments, and accountability.

Third, we must move beyond endless small-scale pilots towards financing solutions that demonstrate results and can reach entire populations. The Justice Financing Framework developed under the Justice Action Coalition offers important proposals for making people-centred justice services financially sustainable.

Finally, justice must become integral to development financing. International financial institutions and development partners should recognize that investments in agriculture, infrastructure, entrepreneurship, gender equality and peacebuilding depend partly on people’s ability to resolve disputes fairly and the credibility of the entire justice system. This is not an argument for diverting resources from development priorities. It is an argument for making those investments more effective and sustainable.
The foundation we cannot afford to ignore

The world faces intersecting crises of inequality, economic uncertainty, democratic distrust and violent conflict. Governments are searching for ways to build more resilient societies, yet one of the most important foundations of resilience remains chronically neglected.
Justice cannot continue to be treated as an institutional afterthought.

A society is not resilient simply because it has strong borders, modern highways or growing financial markets. It is resilient when people trust that grievances can be addressed fairly, rights can be protected, and conflicts can be resolved without violence.

The question is no longer whether we can afford to invest in people-centred justice. It is whether we can afford the economic, social and political consequences of failing to do so. This spotlight provides the argument for the justice case, evidence of what is working and a roadmap of what we must do to make justice work for our societies.

articles.title: Restoring social media access comes at a cost in Gabon
articles.author: Laura
paras: Citizens in Gabon went 248 days without access to Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or YouTube
Originally published on Global Voices
Image of a smartphone showing the Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, and Messenger apps. Screenshot from the DW Afrique YouTube channel.

After more than eight months of government blockage, Gabon has restored its social media access. But it has come at a cost. This reinstatement comes with a tighter regulatory framework and an unprecedented cooperation between the government and various tech giants, raising serious concerns about freedom of expression and privacy.

On February 17, 2026, Gabon’s media regulator, the High Communication Authority (HAC), suspended major social media networks, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube, “until further notice.” According to the regulator, quoted in the daily newspaper L’Essentiel, this measure targeted not only content “undermining national security” but also content involving defamation, cyberbullying, hate speech, and threats to social cohesion.

At first, the suspension had no real impact, with presidential spokesperson Jennyfer Mélodie Sambat claiming it would solely target Meta platforms. However, according to Gabon Media Time, several influencers, content creators, and citizens later experienced access disruptions on YouTube and TikTok, sometimes rendering connections impossible without a bypass tool, such as a virtual private network (VPN).

The global data platform Internet Society Pulse confirmed this observation, revealing major anomalies for Meta, Telegram, TikTok, and YouTube, but not X (formerly Twitter). The online news portal Le360 Afrique consequently reported a surge in VPN usage in the months that followed.
For 248 days, more than 1.84 million individuals, or 71.9 percent of the country’s population of over 2.5 million, were denied regular access to some of the world’s most popular digital platforms.

On October 24, 2026, the HAC lifted this suspension, with Africanews stressing that this ruling didn’t necessarily mean a return to business as usual. It, therefore, remains to be seen whether Gabon, where Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema has been president since September 2023, will restore digital freedoms or establish a new state-controlled online model instead.
From bypassing the suspension to tighter regulatory frameworks

A new legal framework, enacted on February 26, 2026, underpins this reinstatement. According to Gabon Media Time, Ordinance No. 0011/PR/2026 establishes a regulatory framework for digital platform usage, while Ordinance No. 0013/PR/2026 amends the HAC Reorganization Act.

The HAC also invokes a law, enacted on October 5, that ratifies the social media ordinance and establishes a regulatory framework for AI-generated and AI-amplified content, according to reporting by Gabon Review.

What’s more, available data shows that these regulations have introduced joint liability for those who create and share illegal content and require all social media users to provide personal identification information. Purported as tools to combat abuse, these regulations have raised serious concerns about anonymity, personal data protection, and their stifling effect on public debate.
In a country where criticizing public institutions is politically sensitive, the threat of prosecution for posting online could discourage users from expressing dissent.

The issue here isn’t whether the state should combat cyberbullying, disinformation, or hate speech, but rather how. While these are valid concerns, the real worry is whether its measures are transparent, proportionate, and subject to independent scrutiny.
Tech giants enter the regulatory mix

The most decisive development in this saga was undoubtedly the unprecedented cooperation between the government and Big Tech companies. On July 13, 2026, after a meeting at the AI for Good/WSIS summit in Geneva, Gabonese Minister of Digital Economy Mark-Alexandre Doumba announced an agreement with TikTok. Both parties signed a 12-month cooperation agreement, ensuring the platform’s compliance with Gabon’s new regulatory framework.
At the meeting, TikTok presented its Q1 2026 content moderation results, revealing that it had removed more than 23,500 pieces of sensitive content in Gabon.

Meanwhile, the HAC confirmed that it had established an “active cooperation” with TikTok, Meta, and YouTube to “improve content moderation.” The regulator added that, during the suspension, it also held direct discussions with these companies. However, neither the technical details of these exchanges nor the practical operation of the authorities’ reporting tools has been specified.
Find the HAC spokesperson’s full statement here:

These agreements reflect tech companies’ growing influence in digital platform governance. These platforms are also no longer satisfied with merely hosting exchanges between their users; they now shape decisions about what content remains accessible and what does not.

For governments, partnerships with digital platforms provide a direct channel to deal with content they consider harmful, illegal, or threatening to their regime. For tech companies, complying with the state’s requests and distinguishing legitimate moderation from politically motivated censorship poses a significant challenge.
Cooperation is no substitute for transparency
Working alongside digital platforms isn’t inherently problematic. Tech companies ultimately have a responsibility to deal with credible threats, protect vulnerable users, and enforce their own rules.

However, problems arise when the state has direct access to reporting mechanisms — particularly if the public remains unaware of these partnerships. What criteria determine which content is flagged? How are HAC requests processed? Can users challenge a post removal? Are there any safeguards to protect journalists, activists, and government critics?

The line between harmful content and legitimate political expression is often blurred. Without clear procedures, independent monitoring, and an appeals process, critics say these measures risk becoming tools of influence over public debate.

The situation in Gabon represents a much broader trend. As various African states tighten their grip on digital platforms, tech companies face escalating pressure to comply with new national regulations to maintain key market access. The balance of power between governments and tech giants has ultimately become a defining factor in the future of digital rights.
Beyond Gabon: Who is accountable for digital freedom?
Restoring social media access was imperative for Gabonese citizens, journalists, businesspeople, and content creators alike, all of whom suffered under this suspension.

However, access alone doesn’t guarantee freedom. The real test will be whether internet users can participate in online discussions, criticize public policy, and share information without fear of arbitrary sanctions or disproportionate restrictions.

It also depends on Meta, TikTok, and YouTube demonstrating how their cooperation with the Gabonese government complies with international human rights standards, especially freedom of expression, privacy, and access to information.

The current situation in Gabon illustrates how authoritarian control over the digital sphere evolves. Restrictions don’t necessarily end when platform accessibility is restored. Instead, they become regulatory frameworks, personal identification requirements, and tighter government cooperation with private tech companies.

The challenge, therefore, isn’t just about reconnecting citizens to social media, but also about ensuring the digital spaces they return to remain open to criticism, independent information, and public debate.
Although tech giants can negotiate conditions allowing citizens to regain access to digital platforms, they must also ensure those conditions don’t compromise their fundamental freedoms.

articles.title: El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nations
articles.author: Robert Muggah, Richard von Weizsäcker Fellow na Bosch Academy e Co-fundador, Instituto Igarapé; Princeton University
paras: On Nov. 10, 2026, El Salvador President Nayib Bukele posted footage of attack helicopters firing on a compound near Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince.

He had earlier requested, via a social media post in Haitian Creole, the address of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, one of Haiti’s most powerful criminal organizations. Bukele subsequently claimed the operation, conducted with Haitian police, had demolished Joseph’s residence and gang headquarters. As many as 20 people were killed, although Joseph was reportedly absent.

The attack comes amid a flurry of anti-gang operations in Haiti. On Nov. 6, Mathias Saintil, head of the “Boston” gang in Cité Soleil, was killed in a drone strike by a Haitian special task force, prompting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé to declare on the social media platform X “one less gang leader.” Erik Prince, founder of the private military firm Vectus Global, responded: “Nice shot.”

As an expert on organized crime in Latin America and the Caribbean, I believe these operations mark both a dramatic escalation in Haiti’s fight against organized crime and the first overseas test of Bukele’s security model. The intervention is drawing support from some regional leaders and pro-Bukele networks, even as concerns grow over civilian casualties and whether military gains can translate into lasting security.
Rescue mission or military offensive?

El Salvador already had a limited presence in Haiti as one of six countries contributing personnel to the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force, or GSF. The force was authorized in 2025 to help Haitian authorities reclaim cities and streets from violent gangs that control swathes of the impoverished nation. But it remains severely understaffed and has struggled to translate military operations into lasting territorial gains.
Then, in an Oct. 18 gang ambush, four Salvadoran aviation technicians attached to the Gang Suppression Force disappeared. Their burned vehicle was recovered, but their fate remains uncertain.

Either way, Bukele used the incident to justify expanding El Salvador’s military presence in Haiti. Within weeks he had sent roughly 2,500 troops, along with armored vehicles and attack helicopters, in what he initially called a rescue mission.

They joined an already crowded battlefield. Haiti’s police and army operate alongside the GSF, authorized but not commanded by the United Nations. The Haitian task force involved in operations against Saintil also works with former Blackwater CEO Prince’s Vectus Global, while vigilante groups patrol contested neighborhoods. Dozens of armed gangs associated with the gang coalition Viv Ansanm control large parts of Port-au-Prince and operate beyond the capital.

The Gang Suppression Force was authorized by the U.N. Security Council to deploy up to 5,550 personnel, and it currently has roughly 2,000 on the ground. Most of the Salvadoran troops now in Haiti operate outside its command. Haitian Prime Minister Fils-Aimé insists that Haiti directs the operations. Yet neither government has publicly disclosed the agreement specifying Salvadoran authority, rules of engagement or the deployment’s duration.
Without a published deployment agreement, the chain of command and rules for authorizing strikes remain unclear to the public.

Despite President Donald Trump’s support for Bukele, Secretary of State Marco Rubio has distanced Washington from the Salvadoran offensive, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He warned that poor coordination could lead to friendly fire, while U.S. diplomats formally protested the risks to multinational troops and civilian personnel.

Salvadoran authorities dispute American allegations that their gunfire struck the U.S. embassy and endangered multinational troops. They also questioned the credibility of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti.
Uncertain rules of engagement
Haiti’s security crisis is dire.

In recent years, organized violence has reached levels associated with armed conflict. Almost 6,000 people were killed in 2025, and more than 4,000 in the first nine months of 2026. Nearly 1.5 million Haitians have been displaced as of August 2026, and expanded offensives and gang reprisals could drive more from their homes.

An independent legal assessment by the Geneva Academy of International Humanitarian Law and Human Rights classifies fighting between Haitian forces and the Viv Ansanm coalition as a noninternational armed conflict, a legal category that includes civil wars. The International Committee of the Red Cross has separately warned of the risks to civilians, urging all sides to respect international law.

The distinction matters because the rules on lethal force are different in war and policing. Both require civilians to be protected. But in an armed conflict, members of armed groups with combat roles can be targeted even when they pose no immediate threat. In a police operation, simply being suspected of gang membership is not enough to justify killing someone – lethal force is generally allowed only when necessary to protect lives.

Of particular concern is the growing use of explosive drones and helicopter attacks in residential areas. At least 1,243 people were killed in 141 drone operations between March 2025 and January 2026, including at least 60 people reportedly unconnected to gangs, 17 of them children. These operations predated the Salvadoran escalation but demonstrate the risks of using explosive weapons in populated areas.
At the same time, overlapping mandates for foreign troops and private military contractors could complicate investigations into civilian casualties and allegations of unlawful attacks.
Exporting the Bukele model
Some Haitians, exhausted by insecurity, welcome the international intervention.

Crowds have cheered Salvadoran soldiers, waving sticks and chanting Bukele’s name. A prominent Haitian human rights advocate supported the deployment while warning that residents of gang-controlled neighborhoods are not necessarily gang members.

Bukele promotes the offensive through videos of troops and airstrikes amplified by Salvadoran officials and pro-government influencers. Messages in Haitian Creole and Spanish that portray the strikes as victories against gangs closely resemble the government’s widely circulated footage of mass arrests and prison transfers in El Salvador.

Under Bukele, who came to power in 2019, homicides in El Salvador have plummeted, boosting a belief in parts of South America and the Caribbean that an iron fist approach to gang violence is worth the associated cost to human rights. Indeed, security hardliners across Latin America have pointed to El Salvador’s falling homicide rate to justify similar crackdowns. Dominican President Luis Abinader has endorsed the intervention and confirmed logistical and intelligence cooperation.
Yet the Salvadoran model has relied on emergency powers and mass incarceration. Around 1.7% of Salvadorans are imprisoned – by far the highest rate in the world.

Haiti presents greater operational challenges. According to the U.N. Office for Drugs and Crime, gangs hold extensive territory, possess heavy weapons and maintain connections to political and commercial networks. Haitian institutions are weaker, and children are widely recruited into armed groups from a young age. Sustaining territorial gains would require functioning police and courts, along with protection for residents after foreign troops leave.

The expanded Salvadoran presence in Haiti also carries political risks for both governments. Bukele is seeking a third term in February 2027, following constitutional changes that removed presidential term limits.

Salvadoran military casualties could stir criticism at home and pressure him to escalate, particularly with the four Salvadoran technicians whose disappearance prompted the rescue mission still missing. For his part in Haiti, Fils-Aimé has publicly backed the offensive ahead of Haiti’s elections, scheduled for July and October 2027. Civilian casualties or failure to sustain gains could undermine his own government’s credibility.
Beyond military operations
The deployment may foreshadow wider regional security arrangements.
El Salvador belongs to the U.S.-backed Shield of the Americas, a coalition launched by Trump in March 2026 to expand military cooperation against drug cartels and other transnational criminal groups.

The Salvadoran operation in Haiti does not formally fall under that initiative, whose 15 signatories have pledged closer security cooperation. But such partnerships could allow regional governments to deploy forces with American logistical support while limiting direct U.S. military involvement.

Although the Salvadoran operation is the latest high-profile example, I have seen similar cycles working in Haiti since the 2000s. U.N. peacekeepers and Haitian police cleared parts of Cité Soleil between 2007 and 2009, contributing to a decline in kidnappings but failing to deliver lasting security. The U.N. mission later introduced cholera following the 2010 earthquake, killing more than 9,000 people and prompting an eventual apology from the U.N.

Gangs endure because their economic networks survive military offensives. They profit from kidnappings and illicit trade while controlling access to key roads and markets. Removing leaders can weaken organizations without ending these revenue streams.
While the current Salvadoran offensive may deliver short-term security gains, sustaining them will depend on Haitian institutions maintaining control of recovered territory.

Bukele’s intervention is now an overseas test of a security model with considerable political appeal. But its consequences will ultimately be measured by whether Haitians are safer when foreign forces depart.

Robert Muggah is the co-founder of the Igarapé Institute, and a principal of the SecDev Group. He also advises governments, private companies, non-profits and international organizations such as the United Nations, the IMF and the World Bank.

articles.title: Cabo Verde’s presidential election: the stakes in one of Africa’s most stable democracies
articles.author: José Santana Pereira, associate professor, researcher, Universidade de Lisboa
paras: Cape Verde’s presidential election takes place against the backdrop of a democratic record that remains unusual in its regional context. The country, made up of an archipelago of islands off the coast of west Africa, has sustained multiparty competition for more than three decades. It has had peaceful transfers of power and no coups or military takeovers since independence from Portugal in 1975.

Cabo Verde (population 530,000) is a semi-presidential republic in which the president is directly elected. The prime minister is appointed by the president in light of parliamentary election results, and heads a government that is politically accountable to the national assembly.
The president represents the state and safeguards the constitution, while the prime minister and the government conduct public policy.

The presidency nevertheless carries substantial political weight. The president can veto legislation, request constitutional review and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. The office also entails responsibilities in foreign affairs and national defence.

The president is, therefore, not the principal policymaker. However, the way in which these powers are exercised can become particularly consequential when the president and prime minister belong to opposing political camps. This might indeed be the outcome of the 15 November 2026 election.

I am a political communication specialist who has researched the dynamics of Cabo Verde’s presidential elections. In my view the central test for the upcoming poll will be whether the country’s institutions can continue to function effectively while preserving the important distinction between the presidency and the government.

Cape Verde’s political climate is shaped by a recent change of government. The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde returned to office after winning the May 2026 parliamentary election. This ended 10 years of government by the Movement for Democracy, which now forms the opposition.

The African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde’s victory reflected growing voter dissatisfaction with a decade of rule by the Movement for Democracy. This is particularly over poor inter-island transport, economic difficulties, living conditions and public security.

The change of government renewed questions about the balance of power between the president, the new government and parliament, as well as the opposition’s ability to hold the ruling party accountable.
The forthcoming presidential election will, therefore, test not only party loyalties but also voters’ expectations of the presidency and its role in the political system.
The two main contenders are José Maria Neves, backed by the African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde, and Joana Rosa, supported by the Movement for Democracy.
Neves previously served as prime minister between 2001 and 2016. Rosa, a former minister of justice, is the first woman to run for president in Cabo Verde.

They face Antero Tavares, Casimiro de Pina, Gilson Alves and Loisito Sousa. These four offer alternatives to the two parties that have dominated national politics since the introduction of multipartyism in 1991.
These candidates are unlikely, however, to attract support on a scale that would challenge the two main contenders.

Together with political science researchers Danielton Delgado and Susana Rogeiro Nina, I published a paper that offers insight into the dynamics of presidential elections in Cabo Verde. Our 2019 study found that voters didn’t consistently use presidential contests to punish the governing party. Indeed, except in 2011 and 2021, every presidential election in the country was won by the candidate backed by the party that controlled parliament and the executive.

Also, there was not a systematic advantage for independent candidates or candidates backed by smaller parties. The short interval – one to six months – between legislative and presidential elections may help explain this phenomenon, as presidential contests often take place during the governing party’s post-election “honeymoon period”.
What’s different in the upcoming election?

If Neves secures re-election, the presidency and government will be held by figures associated with the same party. This possibility is not unlikely. Since the introduction of multiparty democracy in 1991, every incumbent president who has sought a second term has been re-elected: António Mascarenhas Monteiro in 1996, Pedro Pires in 2006 and Jorge Carlos Fonseca in 2016.
A victory for Neves could play out in one of two ways. It could facilitate cooperation, but it could also raise questions about the president’s independence from the government.

In turn, a victory for Rosa, mirroring the patterns that emerged in 2011 and 2021, would create a situation of divided leadership, with a Movement for Democracy-backed president working alongside an African Party for the Independence of Cabo Verde government.
Such an arrangement is not inherently problematic. Nevertheless, it can require negotiation when constitutional responsibilities and political interests diverge.

Cabo Verde has recent experience of this situation: between November 2021 and the formation of the new government in June 2026, Neves dealt with a Movement for Democracy government. This was led by Ulisses Correia e Silva. Despite their partisan differences, relations were generally characterised by institutional cooperation rather than open confrontation.

In short, whoever wins will face a distinct institutional challenge. Neves will have to balance his party affiliation with the constitutional responsibility to act as head of state. Rosa will need to establish a working relationship with a government led by her political opponents.

articles.title: What lurks ‘Below’ Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show
articles.author: Paul Snelgrove, Professor, Ocean Sciences and Biology, Memorial University of Newfoundland
paras: When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: “THIS I’ve gotta see!”

First, the series showcases coastal Newfoundland, where I was raised and live. Second, I have studied ocean life in the island’s waters for most of my career. Third, it features the marine lab where I work, the Oceans Sciences Centre. And fourth, it stars a giant squid(-ish) animal (sorry Josh Hartnett).
Giant squid have a special place in Newfoundland folklore and science, from early encounters with fishermen to some of the first scientific evidence of their existence.
One key player in this history was the Irish clergyman Moses Harvey, who moved to Newfoundland in 1852 and undertook natural history research in what was then a British colony.
